problems.solution: Each diagonal entry equals twice its original element; output B[i][i]/2. The input guarantees consistency and positive integral solutions. O(N^2) input time, O(N) stored answer.
problems.statement_summary: Reconstruct a positive integer array of length at most 10 from its pairwise-sum matrix, where entry (i,j) equals A[i]+A[j].
problems.review_rationale: The diagonal fixes the array uniquely as B[i][i]/2, so no matrix reconstruction search or general number theory is required. The consistency guarantee removes validation concerns.

problems.solution: Each legal move removes an odd number of negative entries, toggling the parity of their count. A move exists exactly while any negative remains, so the number of moves has fixed parity equal to the original negative count. Odd count wins; deleting any single negative is a winning first move. O(N).
problems.statement_summary: Two players alternately delete a contiguous subarray with product -1 from an array of up to 200000 values in {-1,1}. Determine the winner and a winning first deletion when one exists.
problems.review_rationale: Every move removes an odd number of negatives and therefore flips their count parity. Terminal arrays have zero negatives; all plays have the same move-count parity. A single negative is always a legal move and leaves a losing even-parity state when Alice wins.

problems.solution: Absolute subtraction preserves pairwise parity differences, so mixed parity requires at least one paid modulo. Repeatedly apply X=ceil((min+max)/2) while the values are not all equal and are not exactly {0,1}. Each step halves the magnitude bound. If all values coincide at positive c, apply X=c once; if all are already zero, stop without an invalid X=0 operation. For {0,1}, apply absolute subtraction by 3, modulo 3, then absolute subtraction by 1 twice: {0,1}->{3,2}->{0,2}->{1}->{0}. N>=3 makes every parameter legal. At most ceil(log2 N)+4<=14 operations suffice, O(N log N) time. Same-parity arrays cost zero; mixed parity arrays cost one.
problems.statement_summary: Turn an array of N values in [1,N], with N at most 1000, into zeroes using free absolute subtraction by a common value and paid common-modulus operations. Minimize paid operations and output at most 15 operations.
problems.review_rationale: Free absolute subtraction flips or preserves all parities together, preserving whether both parity classes occur. Midpoint contraction brings maximum magnitude below two in at most ceil(log2 N) steps; the four-operation modulo gadget handles the mixed case. Exhaustive multiset checks for N=3..8 and full ranges through N=1000 confirmed optimal cost, legal parameters and move bound.
issues: Minor implementation clarification corrected: an already all-zero state must terminate instead of attempting the forbidden free-operation parameter X=0.

problems.solution: Maintain S=sum of prefix products and W=sum of last-value times prefix product. Appending x gives fnew=f*(last+x), hence Snew=M*W+s1*S and Wnew=s1*W+s2*S, where s1=sum x and s2=sum x^2. Initialize S=M,W=s1 at length one. Closed-form power sums modulo prime and O(N) transitions satisfy total N<=200000.
problems.statement_summary: Sum the product of adjacent pair sums over every length-N array with entries in [1,M], modulo 998244353. Total N is at most 200000 and M may be 10^9.
problems.review_rationale: Appending a value closes on the zeroth and first weighted moments of the old last element, giving precisely the stated two-state linear recurrence. Brute-force comparison passed all N=2..6 and M=1..4; simultaneous updates are necessary.

problems.solution: Shortest path DP is dp[i]=A[i]+min(dp[i-1],dp[i-2]), so delta[i]=A[i]-max(delta[i-1],0). Delta is in [1-M,M]. Store count per delta; each old delta contributes its count to an interval of M new deltas, updated with a difference array in O(M). Maintain sum of dp over prefixes: Tnew=M*Told+countOld*s1-M*sum(count[d]*max(d,0)). Initialize length2 with count[d]=M for d=1..M, T=2*M*s1. Sum N<=400, M<=400 permits O(NM).
problems.statement_summary: Sum minimum path costs across all length-N arrays of values in [1,M]. A path starts at index 1, ends at N, and advances one or two positions, paying each visited value. N and M are at most 400.
problems.review_rationale: The adjacent-DP difference is bounded independently of path length, and each old difference produces a contiguous interval of new differences. Difference-array aggregation and a separate total-cost moment yield O(NM) rather than enumerating arrays or cost values. Brute-force comparison passed all N=2..6 and M=1..4.

problems.solution: At each current left boundary, compute each remaining sponsor's earliest cut accumulating 1/n of its original total integral. Assign the interval ending at the earliest cut to that sponsor. Every other sponsor loses at most 1/n of its own original total value, so the remaining-value invariant guarantees completion; give the final sponsor the remainder. Precompute trapezoid prefix integrals, locate the current/target segments by binary search, and invert the monotone quadratic within the target segment using a stable root and explicit constant-slope/zero-area handling. O(totalSegments+n^2 log(maxSegments)) time and O(totalSegments) space. Positive total valuation gives positive-width quotas; adequate floating precision is required for the 1e-8 value tolerance.
problems.statement_summary: Partition a billboard into contiguous sections, one per sponsor, so every sponsor receives at least 1/n of its own total value. Each valuation is a nonnegative piecewise-linear function; there are at most 5000 sponsors and 500000 total breakpoints.
problems.review_rationale: The earliest quota cut removes no more than one original quota according to each unchosen sponsor. Inductively enough value remains for every unchosen sponsor, so a solution always exists. Prefix trapezoid integration plus monotone inverse evaluation is feasible; zero-slope/zero-area segments and stable quadratic evaluation need explicit handling.
issues: Removed the unverified 12-second runtime-limit assertion because it is absent from the supplied full source text. The algorithmic feasibility and fairness proof are otherwise sound.
